transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I... I came in because things have been getting a bit strange down at the church. I keep doing these odd things, you see. Like, I'll be standing by the potluck table, just holding the serving spoon up in the air and not moving a muscle. Just frozen there. It was for the macaroni casserole. My sister used to make a wonderful macaroni casserole, used three different kinds of cheese, but she moved out to Ohio... oh, it must be fifteen years ago now. The winters out there are just terrible, I don't know how she stands all that snow. 

But anyway, yes, I just stand there with the spoon. Or... or I'll be folding the exact same stack of paper napkins over and over again while folks are just standing there in line, waiting on me to hand them one. They were the nice napkins, too, the ones with the little scalloped edges. You can't hardly find those at the dollar store anymore, you have to go all the way to the big market in town to get the nice ones... but I just keep folding them, over and over.
When you're standing there holding the spoon or folding the napkins, are you aware of what you're doing and choosing to do it?

Well, no, I... I don't think I'm choosing it. It's more like I just get stuck, you know? Like a record skipping. We used to have this old record player when I was a girl, a big wooden console thing that sat in the parlor. My daddy bought it second-hand from Mr. Henderson down the road. Mr. Henderson had the most beautiful garden, roses as big as your head, but he couldn't hear a lick, so I guess he didn't need the record player anymore. But anyway, no, I don't feel like I'm doing it on purpose. It just happens, and I can't seem to stop until someone taps my shoulder or something.
Do these episodes cause you any distress or interfere with your daily life?

Well, yes, it does bother me quite a bit. I... I've actually had to step back from some of my volunteering at the church, and the choir, too. I just get so mixed up with the plans, and then people have to come behind me and redo everything I was supposed to handle. It makes folks uncomfortable, I can tell. The choir director, Mrs. Gable, she's always been so particular anyway. She wears these big hats on Sundays, the kind with the feathers that stick straight up. I always wonder how she fits in her car with those hats. It's a little blue sedan, I think... or maybe it's silver. My neighbor has a silver car, but it's always covered in pollen this time of year. The yellow dust just gets everywhere, doesn't it? You can't even leave the windows open to get a breeze. But yes, I've had to stop doing a lot of the things I used to do because I just get so turned around.
Do you have any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you try to think about something else?

Well, no, not really. I don't have any thoughts that get stuck like that, not like the record player I was talking about. My mind is mostly pretty quiet, unless I'm trying to remember a recipe. I used to bake all the time, you know. Pies, mostly. Peach pie was my late husband's favorite. He used to say nobody could get the crust quite as flaky as I did. The secret is using ice water, just a few tablespoons, and you have to keep the butter real cold. I'd put the bowl right in the icebox for ten minutes before I started rolling it out. Our old icebox was one of those big Frigidaires with the heavy latch handle. You had to give it a good yank to get it open. My youngest, Tommy, he used to swing on that handle when he was just a little tyke. I told him he was going to pull the whole thing down on top of himself, but you know how boys are. Always climbing on things. But no, I don't have any thoughts that just repeat and repeat.
Do you ever feel like you have to perform certain actions or rituals over and over again?

Well, no, not rituals or anything like that. I don't feel forced to do things over and over. I mean, I do fold the napkins, like we talked about, but I'm not doing it because I *have* to, or because it's a ritual. It's just... well, it's just what happens. But rituals, no. I always thought rituals were more for church, you know? Like the communion. We used to use those tiny little glass cups for the grape juice. The altar guild ladies would spend hours washing them after the service. Such delicate little things. Mary Beth Higgins dropped a whole tray of them once, right on the stone floor by the baptismal font. Sounded like a chandelier crashing down. She was so embarrassed, poor thing. Her face went red as a tomato. Tomatoes did real well this year, didn't they? The heat must have been just right for them. I tried to grow some on my porch, but the squirrels got to them before they even turned pink. Little thieves, they are. But no, I don't have to do any rituals or anything.
Do you have any unwanted thoughts that come into your mind and won't go away?

Well, no, I don't get anything like that. My mind doesn't get stuck on bad thoughts or anything. Unless you count those commercials on the television, I suppose. There's that one with the little green lizard trying to sell car insurance, and the little jingle just gets right in your ear. I think it's a gecko, actually. My grandson Billy had a pet gecko once. He kept it in this big glass tank in his bedroom with a special heat lamp shining on it all day and night. I always told my daughter I was worried that lamp was going to start a fire. You hear about those things on the evening news, you know. Faulty wiring burning a whole house down while people are sleeping. My cousin Martha actually lost her garage to a fire back in, oh, must have been '85 or '86. They said it was an old space heater she left plugged in by accident. She had all her beautiful glass Christmas ornaments stored out there, the ones passed down from our grandmother. They just melted right down into puddles of colored glass. Such a terrible shame, losing family history like that. You can't just go to the store and buy those old ornaments anymore. But anyway, no, I don't have any unwanted thoughts bothering me.
Do you feel like there's something bad that might happen if you don't do something in a certain way or if you stop doing one of these repetitive actions?

Well, no, I don't think so. I don't worry about bad things happening if I don't do something a certain way. I mean, I try to do things right, of course. Like when I hang the laundry out on the line. You have to pin the sheets by the corners, or they catch the wind like a sail and just whip around. I used to love the smell of sheets dried in the sun. It's so much better than that artificial spring breeze scent they put in the dryer sheets nowadays. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she uses those dryer sheets, and the exhaust vent from her dryer blows right toward my kitchen window. It smells like a perfume factory exploded in her basement. She's a lovely woman, though, Mrs. Gable. She brings me a tin of shortbread cookies every Christmas. The kind with the little candied cherries pressed right into the middle. I tried making them once, but my dough was too crumbly. I think I didn't use enough butter. Butter makes everything better, doesn't it? But no, I don't feel like anything bad is going to happen if I don't do things a certain way.
Do you feel an overwhelming urge or impulse to perform these repetitive actions, like folding the napkins or holding the spoon?

Well, no, not an urge. I don't feel forced to do it. I just hold the spoon sometimes. It's just a spoon, you know? We used to have a beautiful set of silver spoons when I was a girl. Real silver, mind you, not that cheap thin metal they sell nowadays that bends right in half when you try to scoop hard ice cream. My mother kept them in a heavy wooden box lined with dark blue velvet. Oh, it was the softest velvet. I used to sneak into the dining room and just rub my fingers on it when she was out in the yard. She only brought that silver out for Easter and Thanksgiving. Easter was always such a big to-do back then. We'd get new dresses, usually pastel colors. Mine was yellow one year, bright yellow like a little baby chick, and I had a matching hat with a shiny white ribbon. The wind caught that hat right off my head as we were walking up the church steps, and it rolled all the way down the hill into a muddy puddle by the road. Ruined the ribbon completely. My mother tried to wash it, but you know how mud stains white satin. It just leaves a dingy brown mark that never quite comes out, even if you soak it in bleach overnight. You might as well just throw it away at that point. But no, I don't get any overwhelming impulses or anything like that.
Do you think that something bad would happen if you weren't folding the napkins or holding the spoon?

Well, no, I don't think anything bad would happen. It's just folding a napkin, after all. Not like leaving the stove on. My sister, Margaret, she left the stove on once when we were living together in our twenties. We had this little apartment above a bakery, and the smell of fresh bread would wake us up every morning at four. It was lovely, but you could never sleep in. Anyway, she boiled a pot of water for tea and just completely forgot about it. Went right out to the market to buy some of those big, juicy tomatoes they used to sell at the corner stand. You can't find tomatoes like that anymore, all mealy and tasteless now, shipped from halfway across the country. But by the time she got back, the water had boiled completely away, and the bottom of the pot was glowing red hot. Ruined the pot entirely. It was one of our good copper-bottom ones, too. We had to throw it out in the alley because it smelled so awful, like burnt metal and ozone. But no, nothing bad would happen if I didn't fold a napkin.
Do you feel like the napkins need to be folded in a specific way or that they have to look a certain way when you're done folding them?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I just fold them. They don't have to be perfect or anything like that. Just folded so they fit in the drawer, you know? My mother used to be very particular about the drawers. She lined all of them with this beautiful floral contact paper. Little pink roses with green vines. It took her hours to cut it just right so the pattern matched up at the seams. She used a special little knife, very sharp. My father used that same knife to cut his cigars. He smoked these big, smelly things he ordered from a catalog. The catalog came in the mail every month, printed on this cheap, thin paper that would turn your fingers black with ink if you held it too long. I used to save the pages and fold them into little paper boats and float them down the gutter after a rainstorm. The water would rush so fast, carrying the boats all the way to the storm drain at the end of the street. You had to be careful not to drop your keys down there, though. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, dropped his car keys down the grate once, and he had to fish them out with a wire coat hanger and a piece of chewed gum. Took him half the afternoon. But no, I don't feel like the napkins have to look a certain way.
Do you feel like the things you repeat, like folding the napkins, need to be done a certain number of times or in a certain pattern?

Well, no, not a certain number of times. I just fold them until I'm done. It's not like counting or anything. I never was much good at counting, not even in school. I left school early, you know, back when I was just a girl. Had to help out at home. My mother took in laundry for the wealthy folks up on the hill, and there was always so much of it. Mountains of white sheets that had to be boiled and scrubbed on a washboard. My knuckles would get so raw and red, especially in the winter when the water in the tub would get freezing cold. We hung the sheets out on the line in the backyard, and sometimes they'd freeze solid before they even dried. They looked like big, stiff ghosts flapping in the wind. The neighbor's dog, a scruffy little terrier mix named Buster, used to bark at them for hours. He had a terrible bark, high-pitched and sharp, like a rusty hinge. His owner was a nice enough fellow, though. Worked at the shoe factory downtown until it closed up in the seventies. He used to bring us scraps of leather, and my father would try to patch his own boots with them. Never held together very long, though, the stitching always came undone in the rain. But no, I don't count the napkins or do them in a pattern. I just fold them.
Do you feel like the things you repeat, like folding the napkins, have to be symmetrical or look orderly when you're done?

Well, no, not really. Symmetrical? I don't think so. I just fold them and put them away. Orderly is nice, I suppose, but I don't obsess over it. My sister Margaret, though, she was obsessed with order. Everything had to be just so. She used to arrange her canned goods alphabetically in the pantry. Apricots, beans, carrots... it drove me crazy when I just wanted to find the soup. We lived in that apartment above the bakery, and she would even arrange the little packets of sugar we'd bring up from the shop. The baker, Mr. Rossi, he was a sweet man, always gave us extra sugar packets. He had a big bushy mustache that would get powdered sugar all in it when he made the jelly donuts. Those donuts were so good, filled with this thick raspberry jam that would squirt out the sides if you bit into it too fast. I ruined a perfectly good white blouse that way once. Had to soak it in lemon juice and leave it in the sun for two days to get the stain out. Lemon juice is wonderful for stains, you know. My mother taught me that. But no, the napkins don't have to be symmetrical or anything. Just folded.
Do you feel like you must fold the napkins or hold the spoon for any reason, even if you don't know why?

Well, no, not really. I don't feel like I *must* do it for any particular reason. I just do it. It's just something to do with my hands, I suppose. My hands are always moving. Even when I'm sitting still, I'm tapping my fingers or picking at my cuticles. My cuticles get so dry in the winter. The skin just flakes right off. I used to use this special lotion, came in a little blue tin. Rose salve, I think it was called. Smelled just like a fresh bouquet of roses. My husband, rest his soul, he brought me a bouquet of red roses for our first anniversary. They were so beautiful, but the thorns were sharp. Pricked my finger right on the thumb, and it bled for a good ten minutes. I had to wrap it in a piece of gauze. We used a lot of gauze back then. Kept a whole box of it in the medicine cabinet, right next to the iodine. Iodine stings so badly when you put it on a cut, but it keeps the infection away. The bottle was made of this dark brown glass, and the liquid was an orange-brown color that would stain your skin for days. But no, I don't feel like I have to fold them for a reason. I just do.
Do you feel like folding the napkins or doing these repetitive actions helps you feel more in control of things?

Well, no, I wouldn't say it's about control. I don't feel out of control, really. I just like to keep my hands busy. Idle hands, you know what they say. My grandmother used to say that all the time. She was always knitting or crocheting something. Afghans, mostly. She made this one afghan, it was all these little squares sewn together. Granny squares, they called them. Every color of the rainbow. She used up all her scrap yarn on it. Some of the yarn was scratchy wool, the kind that makes your neck itch if you wear a sweater made out of it. I had a yellow wool sweater once, a cardigan with little pearl buttons. I lost one of the buttons on the bus going downtown to buy groceries. The bus driver was a grumpy man, always tapping his watch if you took too long getting your fare out. Fares used to be just a nickel. Can you imagine? A nickel wouldn't buy you anything nowadays. Not even a piece of hard candy at the drugstore. The drugstore on the corner used to have those big glass jars full of candy... peppermint sticks and lemon drops. The lemon drops were my favorite. But no, folding the napkins doesn't make me feel in control or anything like that.
Do you feel like the napkins or any other things you repeat need to be done perfectly?

Perfectly? Oh, heavens no. I don't think anything in this world is truly perfect, do you? I just fold them so they're put away. It doesn't have to be exact. Exactness is such a tiring thing. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she tried to keep a perfect lawn. Every blade of grass had to be exactly the same height. She'd be out there with these little hand shears, trimming the edges by the sidewalk. It was a concrete sidewalk, the kind with the sparkly bits in it that caught the sun. We used to draw hopscotch boards on it with chalk when we were little girls. Pink and blue chalk. The blue always washed away faster in the rain, for some reason. We had such heavy rain that spring, the river flooded over the banks and washed out the old wooden bridge. They had to build a new one out of steel. It was painted this awful shade of green, like pea soup. I never did like pea soup, even when my mother made it with ham hocks. But no, the folding doesn't have to be perfect at all. Just done.
Do you feel like the things you do, like folding the napkins, have to be done in a way that looks neat or organized?

Neat? Well, I suppose I like things tidy, but it doesn't have to be perfectly organized. I just fold them and set them down. It's not about making a display out of them. Displays remind me of those department store windows downtown during Christmas time. They used to go all out, you know? The mannequins would be dressed in these heavy velvet coats with fur collars. Real fur, back then. Mink, usually. My aunt had a mink stole she wore to church on Sundays. She always sat in the third pew on the left, right under the stained glass window that showed Noah's Ark. The sunlight would come through the blue glass and make the whole aisle look like it was underwater. I always liked the story of Noah's Ark, all those animals marching in two by two. Two elephants, two giraffes. Giraffes have such long necks, I wonder how they don't get a sore throat more often. When I get a sore throat, I like to drink hot tea with a spoonful of honey and a squeeze of lemon. But no, I don't need the napkins to look a certain way. I just fold them to keep my hands moving.
Do you feel like the napkins need to be folded in a way that makes them look balanced or even on both sides?

Balanced? Oh, I don't really pay attention to that. I just fold them in half, or maybe in quarters if they're the big ones, and that's that. Balance is tricky, though, isn't it? Like trying to balance on a bicycle when you're first learning. My brother Tommy taught me how to ride on this old red Schwinn he found at a rummage sale. It had a banana seat, the kind with the silver sparkles in the vinyl. He used to ride me on the handlebars down to the creek to catch pollywogs in a glass mayonnaise jar. We'd punch holes in the lid with a rusty nail so they could breathe. You have to be careful with rusty nails, you know. You step on one and you have to get a tetanus shot. Those shots hurt like the dickens, right in the meaty part of your arm. My arm ached for three days after I got one when I stepped on a roofing tack. They were putting a new roof on the Methodist church at the time, black asphalt shingles that smelled like tar in the hot July sun. The smell of tar always makes me think of road work... but no, I don't really worry if the napkins are even on both sides or not.
Do you feel like something is compelling you to fold the napkins or hold the spoon, even if you don't understand why?

Compelling me? Like something forcing me? Oh, no, nothing like that. I don't feel pushed by anything. I just do it because my hands are there. Hands are funny things, aren't they? You look at them one day and they're all smooth, and the next they're covered in those little brown spots. Liver spots, my mother called them, though I don't know what they have to do with livers. We used to have liver and onions every Tuesday night for supper. My father insisted on it. He said it put iron in your blood. He worked at the steel mill, down by the river, so he knew all about iron. He'd come home with his face just black with soot, and he'd wash up at the kitchen sink with this gritty soap that smelled like pine needles. We had a big pine tree in the front yard, right by the porch. The neighborhood kids would collect the pinecones and paint them gold for Christmas ornaments. We'd string them up with popcorn and cranberries. Cranberries are so tart, you have to use a whole cup of sugar if you want to make a decent sauce out of them. But no, nobody's making me hold the spoon or fold things. It's just something to do.
Do you feel anxious or worried about something happening if you stop folding the napkins or holding the spoon?

Anxious? Oh, no, I don't get worried about stopping. I could stop right now if I wanted to. It's just... well, stopping reminds me of the bus stop at the end of our street when I was a girl. The number 42 bus used to come by every half hour, regular as clockwork. The driver was a man named Mr. Henderson. He had this magnificent handlebar mustache, the kind you don't see anymore. He said he waxed it every morning with beeswax. Beeswax is wonderful for polishing furniture, too. My grandmother had this beautiful cherry wood dining table that she'd polish until you could see your reflection in it. We'd sit around that table on Sundays and eat pot roast with carrots and potatoes. The potatoes were always the little red ones, boiled with their skins still on. They have more vitamins in the skins, you know. That's what they say on the television programs, anyway. I like watching the cooking shows, especially the ones where they bake cakes. The way they pipe the frosting on so perfectly... it's like art. But no, I'm not worried about anything bad happening if I put the napkin down. I'm fine.
Do you feel like the things you repeat, such as folding the napkins, have to be done in a precise or symmetrical way?

Precise? Symmetrical? Oh, I don't know about all that. I'm not a mathematician or anything. I just fold them. Mathematics was never my strong suit in school, anyway. I liked spelling much better. We used to have spelling bees every Friday afternoon in Mrs. Gable's class. I won a blue ribbon once for spelling "chrysanthemum." It's a tricky word, all those letters. My mother grew the most beautiful yellow chrysanthemums in her garden out back. They bloomed right around the time the leaves started turning in October. October is such a crisp month, isn't it? The air smells like woodsmoke. Our neighbor, Mr. Abernathy, used to burn his leaves in a big metal barrel in the alley. You can't do that anymore, against the city ordinance, they say. They come by with those big trucks that sweep the street instead. The bristles on those brushes are so thick, I always wonder what they're made of. Maybe some kind of heavy plastic? Plastic is everywhere now. When I was little, everything came in glass bottles. The milkman would leave glass bottles on the porch, and the cream would rise right up to the top. You had to shake it before you poured it on your cereal. I liked cornflakes best. But no, I don't worry about folding things in a precise way. Just fold them and that's that.

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about OCD symptoms (compulsions driven by anxiety/fears of bad things happening), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer: Well, no, I don't think so. I don't worry about bad things happening if I don't do something a certain way. I mean, I try to do things right, of course. Like when I hang the laundry out on the line. You have to pin the sheets by the corners, or they catch the wind like a sail and just whip around. I used to love the smell of sheets dried in the sun. It's so much better than that artificial spring breeze scent they put in the dryer sheets nowadays. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she uses those dryer sheets, and the exhaust vent from her dryer blows right toward my kitchen window. It smells like a perfume factory exploded in her basement. She's a lovely woman, though, Mrs. Gable. She brings me a tin of shortbread cookies every Christmas. The kind with the little candied cherries pressed right into the middle. I tried making them once, but my dough was too crumbly. I think I didn't use enough butter. Butter makes everything better, doesn't it? But no, I don't feel like anything bad is going to happen if I don't do things a certain way.

doctor.intent: determine presence of compulsions to understand potential diagnosis of obsessive-compulsive disorder or other related conditions
doctor.question: Do you feel an overwhelming urge or impulse to perform these repetitive actions, like folding the napkins or holding the spoon?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about overwhelming urges or impulses to perform repetitive actions (exploring compulsions/OCD). My profile covers disorganized behavior (doing odd things without a clear purpose or urge) and disorganized speech, but does not include having overwhelming urges or impulses to perform these actions.

patient.answer: Well, no, not an urge. I don't feel forced to do it. I just hold the spoon sometimes. It's just a spoon, you know? We used to have a beautiful set of silver spoons when I was a girl. Real silver, mind you, not that cheap thin metal they sell nowadays that bends right in half when you try to scoop hard ice cream. My mother kept them in a heavy wooden box lined with dark blue velvet. Oh, it was the softest velvet. I used to sneak into the dining room and just rub my fingers on it when she was out in the yard. She only brought that silver out for Easter and Thanksgiving. Easter was always such a big to-do back then. We'd get new dresses, usually pastel colors. Mine was yellow one year, bright yellow like a little baby chick, and I had a matching hat with a shiny white ribbon. The wind caught that hat right off my head as we were walking up the church steps, and it rolled all the way down the hill into a muddy puddle by the road. Ruined the ribbon completely. My mother tried to wash it, but you know how mud stains white satin. It just leaves a dingy brown mark that never quite comes out, even if you soak it in bleach overnight. You might as well just throw it away at that point. But no, I don't get any overwhelming impulses or anything like that.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's repetitive actions are aimed at preventing some dreaded event
doctor.question: Do you think that something bad would happen if you weren't folding the napkins or holding the spoon?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient believes something bad will happen if they don't perform the repetitive actions (checking for obsessive-compulsive fears/beliefs). This does not match any of the provided symptom profiles for this patient, which cover disorganized behavior, disorganized speech, functional impairment, duration, and psychotic symptoms duration.

patient.answer: Well, no, I don't think anything bad would happen. It's just folding a napkin, after all. Not like leaving the stove on. My sister, Margaret, she left the stove on once when we were living together in our twenties. We had this little apartment above a bakery, and the smell of fresh bread would wake us up every morning at four. It was lovely, but you could never sleep in. Anyway, she boiled a pot of water for tea and just completely forgot about it. Went right out to the market to buy some of those big, juicy tomatoes they used to sell at the corner stand. You can't find tomatoes like that anymore, all mealy and tasteless now, shipped from halfway across the country. But by the time she got back, the water had boiled completely away, and the bottom of the pot was glowing red hot. Ruined the pot entirely. It was one of our good copper-bottom ones, too. We had to throw it out in the alley because it smelled so awful, like burnt metal and ozone. But no, nothing bad would happen if I didn't fold a napkin.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's repetitive behaviors are driven by a need for symmetry or exactness
doctor.question: Do you feel like the napkins need to be folded in a specific way or that they have to look a certain way when you're done folding them?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient feels a need for the napkins to be folded in a specific or exact way (checking for obsessive-compulsive traits/symmetry/exactness). The patient's symptom profile covers Disorganized Abnormal Behavior (which involves folding the same stack over and over, but not necessarily a need for a specific/exact way or rules) and Disorganized Thinking/Speech, Functional Impairment, and Duration. The specific question about needing things to be folded in a specific way or look a certain way is not covered by the profile.

patient.answer: Well, no, not really. I mean, I just fold them. They don't have to be perfect or anything like that. Just folded so they fit in the drawer, you know? My mother used to be very particular about the drawers. She lined all of them with this beautiful floral contact paper. Little pink roses with green vines. It took her hours to cut it just right so the pattern matched up at the seams. She used a special little knife, very sharp. My father used that same knife to cut his cigars. He smoked these big, smelly things he ordered from a catalog. The catalog came in the mail every month, printed on this cheap, thin paper that would turn your fingers black with ink if you held it too long. I used to save the pages and fold them into little paper boats and float them down the gutter after a rainstorm. The water would rush so fast, carrying the boats all the way to the storm drain at the end of the street. You had to be careful not to drop your keys down there, though. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, dropped his car keys down the grate once, and he had to fish them out with a wire coat hanger and a piece of chewed gum. Took him half the afternoon. But no, I don't feel like the napkins have to look a certain way.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's repetitive behaviors are driven by a need for symmetry or exactness
doctor.question: Do you feel like the things you repeat, like folding the napkins, need to be done a certain number of times or in a certain pattern?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the repetitive actions (folding napkins) need to be done a certain number of times or in a specific pattern, which is a symptom of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (compulsions). This is not covered by any of my symptom profiles.

patient.answer: Well, no, not a certain number of times. I just fold them until I'm done. It's not like counting or anything. I never was much good at counting, not even in school. I left school early, you know, back when I was just a girl. Had to help out at home. My mother took in laundry for the wealthy folks up on the hill, and there was always so much of it. Mountains of white sheets that had to be boiled and scrubbed on a washboard. My knuckles would get so raw and red, especially in the winter when the water in the tub would get freezing cold. We hung the sheets out on the line in the backyard, and sometimes they'd freeze solid before they even dried. They looked like big, stiff ghosts flapping in the wind. The neighbor's dog, a scruffy little terrier mix named Buster, used to bark at them for hours. He had a terrible bark, high-pitched and sharp, like a rusty hinge. His owner was a nice enough fellow, though. Worked at the shoe factory downtown until it closed up in the seventies. He used to bring us scraps of leather, and my father would try to patch his own boots with them. Never held together very long, though, the stitching always came undone in the rain. But no, I don't count the napkins or do them in a pattern. I just fold them.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's repetitive actions are driven by a need for symmetry or order
doctor.question: Do you feel like the things you repeat, like folding the napkins, have to be symmetrical or look orderly when you're done?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (specifically, a need for symmetry or exactness in repetitive behaviors). This is not covered by the patient's Schizophrenia symptom profile, which includes disorganized behavior, disorganized speech, functional impairment, duration, and psychotic symptoms duration.

patient.answer: Well, no, not really. Symmetrical? I don't think so. I just fold them and put them away. Orderly is nice, I suppose, but I don't obsess over it. My sister Margaret, though, she was obsessed with order. Everything had to be just so. She used to arrange her canned goods alphabetically in the pantry. Apricots, beans, carrots... it drove me crazy when I just wanted to find the soup. We lived in that apartment above the bakery, and she would even arrange the little packets of sugar we'd bring up from the shop. The baker, Mr. Rossi, he was a sweet man, always gave us extra sugar packets. He had a big bushy mustache that would get powdered sugar all in it when he made the jelly donuts. Those donuts were so good, filled with this thick raspberry jam that would squirt out the sides if you bit into it too fast. I ruined a perfectly good white blouse that way once. Had to soak it in lemon juice and leave it in the sun for two days to get the stain out. Lemon juice is wonderful for stains, you know. My mother taught me that. But no, the napkins don't have to be symmetrical or anything. Just folded.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any mental compulsion to perform the repetitive actions
doctor.question: Do you feel like you must fold the napkins or hold the spoon for any reason, even if you don't know why?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient feels a compulsion or uncontrollable urge to perform the repetitive behaviors (folding napkins, holding the spoon) for any reason. This is probing for OCD-like compulsions. While the behaviors are part of the patient's Disorganized Abnormal Behavior (S022), the specific question about feeling a *compulsion* or *must do it for any reason* is not covered by the symptom profile, which describes the behavior as a manifestation of disorganized motor control rather than an obsessive compulsion.

patient.answer: Well, no, not really. I don't feel like I *must* do it for any particular reason. I just do it. It's just something to do with my hands, I suppose. My hands are always moving. Even when I'm sitting still, I'm tapping my fingers or picking at my cuticles. My cuticles get so dry in the winter. The skin just flakes right off. I used to use this special lotion, came in a little blue tin. Rose salve, I think it was called. Smelled just like a fresh bouquet of roses. My husband, rest his soul, he brought me a bouquet of red roses for our first anniversary. They were so beautiful, but the thorns were sharp. Pricked my finger right on the thumb, and it bled for a good ten minutes. I had to wrap it in a piece of gauze. We used a lot of gauze back then. Kept a whole box of it in the medicine cabinet, right next to the iodine. Iodine stings so badly when you put it on a cut, but it keeps the infection away. The bottle was made of this dark brown glass, and the liquid was an orange-brown color that would stain your skin for days. But no, I don't feel like I have to fold them for a reason. I just do.

doctor.intent: Determine if patient's actions are driven by a need for control or perfection
doctor.question: Do you feel like folding the napkins or doing these repetitive actions helps you feel more in control of things?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the repetitive actions help the patient feel more in control, which is exploring potential obsessive-compulsive motivations. This is not covered by the symptom profile, which includes disorganized behavior, disorganized speech, functional impairment, and duration.

patient.answer: Well, no, I wouldn't say it's about control. I don't feel out of control, really. I just like to keep my hands busy. Idle hands, you know what they say. My grandmother used to say that all the time. She was always knitting or crocheting something. Afghans, mostly. She made this one afghan, it was all these little squares sewn together. Granny squares, they called them. Every color of the rainbow. She used up all her scrap yarn on it. Some of the yarn was scratchy wool, the kind that makes your neck itch if you wear a sweater made out of it. I had a yellow wool sweater once, a cardigan with little pearl buttons. I lost one of the buttons on the bus going downtown to buy groceries. The bus driver was a grumpy man, always tapping his watch if you took too long getting your fare out. Fares used to be just a nickel. Can you imagine? A nickel wouldn't buy you anything nowadays. Not even a piece of hard candy at the drugstore. The drugstore on the corner used to have those big glass jars full of candy... peppermint sticks and lemon drops. The lemon drops were my favorite. But no, folding the napkins doesn't make me feel in control or anything like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's repetitive actions are driven by a need for perfection
doctor.question: Do you feel like the napkins or any other things you repeat need to be done perfectly?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about perfectionism or needing things to be done perfectly in relation to the repetitive actions (folding napkins). This is inquiring about obsessive-compulsive traits (perfectionism/exactness), which is not covered by my symptom profile (Disorganized Behavior, Disorganized Speech, Functional Impairment, Duration).

patient.answer: Perfectly? Oh, heavens no. I don't think anything in this world is truly perfect, do you? I just fold them so they're put away. It doesn't have to be exact. Exactness is such a tiring thing. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she tried to keep a perfect lawn. Every blade of grass had to be exactly the same height. She'd be out there with these little hand shears, trimming the edges by the sidewalk. It was a concrete sidewalk, the kind with the sparkly bits in it that caught the sun. We used to draw hopscotch boards on it with chalk when we were little girls. Pink and blue chalk. The blue always washed away faster in the rain, for some reason. We had such heavy rain that spring, the river flooded over the banks and washed out the old wooden bridge. They had to build a new one out of steel. It was painted this awful shade of green, like pea soup. I never did like pea soup, even when my mother made it with ham hocks. But no, the folding doesn't have to be perfect at all. Just done.

doctor.intent: Determine if patient's repetitive actions are driven by a need for symmetry or order
doctor.question: Do you feel like the things you do, like folding the napkins, have to be done in a way that looks neat or organized?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the repetitive behaviors (like folding napkins) need to be neat or organized, which is probing for OCD-like compulsions or perfectionism. This does not map to any of my schizophrenia symptom profiles (S022 Disorganized Behavior, S021 Disorganized Speech, Functional Impairment, Duration, Psychotic Symptoms Duration).

patient.answer: Neat? Well, I suppose I like things tidy, but it doesn't have to be perfectly organized. I just fold them and set them down. It's not about making a display out of them. Displays remind me of those department store windows downtown during Christmas time. They used to go all out, you know? The mannequins would be dressed in these heavy velvet coats with fur collars. Real fur, back then. Mink, usually. My aunt had a mink stole she wore to church on Sundays. She always sat in the third pew on the left, right under the stained glass window that showed Noah's Ark. The sunlight would come through the blue glass and make the whole aisle look like it was underwater. I always liked the story of Noah's Ark, all those animals marching in two by two. Two elephants, two giraffes. Giraffes have such long necks, I wonder how they don't get a sore throat more often. When I get a sore throat, I like to drink hot tea with a spoonful of honey and a squeeze of lemon. But no, I don't need the napkins to look a certain way. I just fold them to keep my hands moving.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's actions are driven by a need for symmetry or exactness
doctor.question: Do you feel like the napkins need to be folded in a way that makes them look balanced or even on both sides?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the need for symmetry or exactness in repetitive behaviors (checking for OCD-like traits), which is not covered by any of the symptom profiles.

patient.answer: Balanced? Oh, I don't really pay attention to that. I just fold them in half, or maybe in quarters if they're the big ones, and that's that. Balance is tricky, though, isn't it? Like trying to balance on a bicycle when you're first learning. My brother Tommy taught me how to ride on this old red Schwinn he found at a rummage sale. It had a banana seat, the kind with the silver sparkles in the vinyl. He used to ride me on the handlebars down to the creek to catch pollywogs in a glass mayonnaise jar. We'd punch holes in the lid with a rusty nail so they could breathe. You have to be careful with rusty nails, you know. You step on one and you have to get a tetanus shot. Those shots hurt like the dickens, right in the meaty part of your arm. My arm ached for three days after I got one when I stepped on a roofing tack. They were putting a new roof on the Methodist church at the time, black asphalt shingles that smelled like tar in the hot July sun. The smell of tar always makes me think of road work... but no, I don't really worry if the napkins are even on both sides or not.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's repetitive actions are a result of obsessive thoughts or compulsions
doctor.question: Do you feel like something is compelling you to fold the napkins or hold the spoon, even if you don't understand why?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if there is a compulsion or an uncontrollable urge to perform the behaviors (folding napkins, holding the spoon), which is assessing for symptoms of OCD (compulsions). The symptom profile contains Disorganized Abnormal Behavior, Disorganized Thinking/Speech, Functional Impairment, Duration, and Psychotic Symptoms Duration, but does not have an item for compulsions or the subjective feeling of being compelled.

patient.answer: Compelling me? Like something forcing me? Oh, no, nothing like that. I don't feel pushed by anything. I just do it because my hands are there. Hands are funny things, aren't they? You look at them one day and they're all smooth, and the next they're covered in those little brown spots. Liver spots, my mother called them, though I don't know what they have to do with livers. We used to have liver and onions every Tuesday night for supper. My father insisted on it. He said it put iron in your blood. He worked at the steel mill, down by the river, so he knew all about iron. He'd come home with his face just black with soot, and he'd wash up at the kitchen sink with this gritty soap that smelled like pine needles. We had a big pine tree in the front yard, right by the porch. The neighborhood kids would collect the pinecones and paint them gold for Christmas ornaments. We'd string them up with popcorn and cranberries. Cranberries are so tart, you have to use a whole cup of sugar if you want to make a decent sauce out of them. But no, nobody's making me hold the spoon or fold things. It's just something to do.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's actions are driven by a fear of harm or bad consequences if they don't perform the repetitive actions
doctor.question: Do you feel anxious or worried about something happening if you stop folding the napkins or holding the spoon?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I feel anxious or worried about stopping the behavior, which assesses for OCD-like obsessions/compulsions or anxiety disorders. This is not covered by my symptom profile (which only includes disorganized behavior, disorganized speech, functional impairment, and duration).

patient.answer: Anxious? Oh, no, I don't get worried about stopping. I could stop right now if I wanted to. It's just... well, stopping reminds me of the bus stop at the end of our street when I was a girl. The number 42 bus used to come by every half hour, regular as clockwork. The driver was a man named Mr. Henderson. He had this magnificent handlebar mustache, the kind you don't see anymore. He said he waxed it every morning with beeswax. Beeswax is wonderful for polishing furniture, too. My grandmother had this beautiful cherry wood dining table that she'd polish until you could see your reflection in it. We'd sit around that table on Sundays and eat pot roast with carrots and potatoes. The potatoes were always the little red ones, boiled with their skins still on. They have more vitamins in the skins, you know. That's what they say on the television programs, anyway. I like watching the cooking shows, especially the ones where they bake cakes. The way they pipe the frosting on so perfectly... it's like art. But no, I'm not worried about anything bad happening if I put the napkin down. I'm fine.

doctor.intent: determine if patient's actions are driven by a need for symmetry or exactness
doctor.question: Do you feel like the things you repeat, such as folding the napkins, have to be done in a precise or symmetrical way?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the repetitive behaviors (folding napkins) need to be done in a precise or symmetrical way, which is assessing for obsessive-compulsive traits (symmetry/exactness). This is not covered by the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer: Precise? Symmetrical? Oh, I don't know about all that. I'm not a mathematician or anything. I just fold them. Mathematics was never my strong suit in school, anyway. I liked spelling much better. We used to have spelling bees every Friday afternoon in Mrs. Gable's class. I won a blue ribbon once for spelling "chrysanthemum." It's a tricky word, all those letters. My mother grew the most beautiful yellow chrysanthemums in her garden out back. They bloomed right around the time the leaves started turning in October. October is such a crisp month, isn't it? The air smells like woodsmoke. Our neighbor, Mr. Abernathy, used to burn his leaves in a big metal barrel in the alley. You can't do that anymore, against the city ordinance, they say. They come by with those big trucks that sweep the street instead. The bristles on those brushes are so thick, I always wonder what they're made of. Maybe some kind of heavy plastic? Plastic is everywhere now. When I was little, everything came in glass bottles. The milkman would leave glass bottles on the porch, and the cream would rise right up to the top. You had to shake it before you poured it on your cereal. I liked cornflakes best. But no, I don't worry about folding things in a precise way. Just fold them and that's that.
